subtopic: Global cultures: eye contact, personal space, directness and time
passage: Zanele arrived at the library meeting room in Hamburg at half past ten. The project group had started at ten sharp. Selin looked at the clock, then at Zanele, and said only, "We've begun the first section." Back home in Durban, ten o'clock meant people drifted in by eleven and nobody minded. Here, three classmates who had waited exchanged a look. Zanele's face went hot, and Zanele stayed to the end without a word. Afterwards Zanele said, "I didn't understand how strict the clock is here. I'm sorry." Selin nodded. "If you're running late, send a message before, even five minutes." Zanele set the alarm fifteen minutes early, and the next week arrived first.

qa.q: How late was Zanele to the meeting?
qa.a: Zanele arrived at half past ten for a group that had started at ten sharp.

qa.q: How did Zanele feel when Selin looked at the clock?
qa.a: Embarrassed and worried about seeming unreliable; the face went hot.

qa.q: What could Zanele do whenever running late in future?
qa.a: Send a message before, even for five minutes, and leave earlier.

qa.q: How might Selin and the classmates have seen the late arrival?
qa.a: As a lack of respect for their time, since they had waited from ten, though Zanele meant no offence.

grounding: A student used to flexible timings arrives half an hour late in a strict-time setting, then learns the local clock and to message ahead.

subtopic: Global cultures: eye contact, personal space, directness and time
passage: At the engineering office in Frankfurt, the induction started at nine. Saurabh, an intern from Jaipur, walked in at half past nine, smiling and apologising about the tram. Vasudha, the HR coordinator, was already handing badges to the others. "We began at nine," Vasudha said evenly. "Here, arriving on time means being there before the start." Saurabh's smile faded. Back home, half an hour late for a family gathering hardly counted. "I didn't know," Saurabh said. "Could you tell me what I missed, and how to let you know if something delays me?" Vasudha handed over the printout and wrote a phone number at the top. "Call before, not after." Next morning Saurabh was in the lobby at ten to nine.

qa.q: What time did the induction start?
qa.a: The induction started at nine.

qa.q: What was Saurabh feeling when the smile faded?
qa.a: Embarrassed and uneasy, realising that being late had been taken seriously.

qa.q: What small steps could Saurabh take to avoid offence?
qa.a: Arrive before the start and call ahead if something delays the journey.

qa.q: How does Vasudha see arriving on time?
qa.a: As being there before the start, which respects everyone's schedule.

grounding: A student used to flexible timings arrives late at a strict-time workplace and learns to arrive early and tell people ahead.

subtopic: Global cultures: eye contact, personal space, directness and time
passage: Sahil, sit. Let me tell you about my first review in Rotterdam. I was twenty-five and proud of my report. My manager, Ms. de Vries, said flatly, "This section is unclear and the numbers don't match. Redo it." My ears rang. Back in my office at home, criticism came wrapped in three compliments. I went to the pantry and thought I was being fired. Then I made myself go back and ask, "Is this about the report, or about me?" She looked surprised. "The report. The rest is strong." That sentence gave me the rest of my day. I fixed the numbers, and I learned to hear the content and let the tone pass. Nitin, that's me, still learning at fifty.

qa.q: Where did Nitin have the first review?
qa.a: Nitin's first review was in Rotterdam.

qa.q: How did Nitin feel after the blunt feedback, and what shows it?
qa.a: Hurt and afraid; the ringing ears and the thought of being fired show it.

qa.q: What choice did Nitin make that changed the day?
qa.a: Going back to ask whether the criticism was about the report or about Nitin, which separated tone from content.

qa.q: How might Ms. de Vries have seen her own feedback?
qa.a: As plain clarity about the report, not an attack; she looked surprised at the question.

grounding: A young professional is hurt by blunt criticism from a foreign manager, asks about intent and separates tone from content.

subtopic: Global cultures: eye contact, personal space, directness and time
passage: The video call kept freezing, and the report was due at six. Baljeet, the Canadian manager, said, "Anand, the second section is weak. Rewrite it before you send." Then the screen froze on Baljeet's frowning face. Anand felt the words land like a slap; he had stayed late for three nights. He wanted to close the laptop. Instead he typed in the chat, "Can I check what you mean? Is the whole report weak, or only the second section?" The reply came after a minute. "Only the second. The rest is strong. Sorry, I'm quick with criticism." Anand exhaled, pulled up the section and rewrote it with time to spare.

qa.q: What time was the report due?
qa.a: The report was due at six.

qa.q: How did Anand feel on hearing the second section was weak?
qa.a: Hurt, like a slap, after three late nights; the wish to close the laptop shows it.

qa.q: Which question helped Anand, and why?
qa.a: Asking whether the whole report or only the second section was weak, because it separated tone from content and showed what to fix.

qa.q: What might Baljeet have meant by the comment?
qa.a: Only clarity about one section, meant to help; Baljeet is quick with criticism and did not intend hurt.

grounding: A young professional hurt by blunt criticism from a foreign manager asks about intent and separates tone from content.

subtopic: Global cultures: eye contact, personal space, directness and time
passage: Dear Tejas, Week two in Kyoto and I have learnt more from asking than from any guidebook. On day one I nearly handed my host a gift with one hand, until Emi, the assistant, smiled and showed me she uses both hands. I asked what to wear to the tea house, and Emi said plain clothes, covered shoulders and clean socks, since shoes come off. At the office nobody expected me to bow perfectly, but they seemed to like that I tried. I stopped assuming a short answer meant coldness; Emi told me it is just her way of being polite. Last night my host invited me home for dinner. My whole lesson: ask before you guess. Write soon. Manoj

qa.q: Who showed Manoj how to hand over the gift?
qa.a: Emi showed Manoj that both hands are used.

qa.q: What is Manoj feeling toward the people in Kyoto?
qa.a: Warmth and curiosity; Manoj is grateful for Emi's help and pleased to be invited to dinner.

qa.q: What habit prevented errors for Manoj?
qa.a: Asking locals before guessing at what a greeting, gift or answer means.

qa.q: How might Emi have felt seeing Manoj ask about clothes and gifts?
qa.a: Pleased and respected, since Emi smiled and helped and did not seem to mind the questions.

grounding: A traveller asks locals about gifts, dress and manners before assuming meaning, and is welcomed with warmth.

subtopic: Global cultures: eye contact, personal space, directness and time
passage: Thanks for having me, Alka. I'm Ankita, and my first week in Bali was all about asking. I didn't want to assume anything. Wayan, who runs my guesthouse, told me that at the temple I'd need a sarong and sash, and to hand things over with my right hand. I asked about the little offerings on the pavement, and Wayan laughed and said people usually step around them. I was so afraid of causing offence that I asked everything: how to greet people, what to bring if a family invites you to a ceremony. Wayan said a small gift of fruit was fine. By the end of the week I was invited to eat with the family. Curiosity opens doors faster than confidence.

qa.q: What did Wayan say Ankita would need at the temple?
qa.a: Wayan said Ankita would need a sarong and sash.

qa.q: Why did Ankita ask so many questions, and how did it feel?
qa.a: Ankita feared causing offence and wanted to understand instead of assume, so it felt nervous but eager.

qa.q: What would you advise a traveller arriving in a new country?
qa.a: Ask locals about greetings, gifts and dress before assuming meaning, and stay curious.

qa.q: How might Wayan have felt about Ankita's questions?
qa.a: Welcomed and respected, judging by the laugh and the invitation to eat with the family.

grounding: A traveller asks a local about greetings, gifts and dress before assuming meaning, and wins warmth.

subtopic: Global cultures: eye contact, personal space, directness and time
passage: Thanks for asking, Rajni. When I moved to Manchester, my flatmate Owen kept looking puzzled when I answered questions with a head wobble. I hadn't noticed I was doing it. I explained, laughing, that it means something like okay or I hear you, and Owen said, "So, yes?" We settled on me saying yes out loud as well. Then there was me on the phone to my mother in the shared kitchen, loud as at home; Owen was polite until I noticed his face, and I took the call to my room. I also learnt not to ask a new colleague about salary in the first week, which I thought was friendly. Not everyone from home does these things, but I did, and a bit of explaining and adapting helped us both enjoy it. Pradeep

qa.q: Where did Pradeep move to?
qa.a: Pradeep moved to Manchester.

qa.q: What did Pradeep feel on noticing Owen's face during the phone call?
qa.a: Self-conscious but considerate; seeing the face made Pradeep take the call to the bedroom.

qa.q: What did Pradeep and Owen do about the head wobble?
qa.a: They settled on Pradeep saying yes out loud as well.

qa.q: How might Owen have felt about the head wobble at first?
qa.a: Puzzled, unsure whether it meant yes or no, which is why Owen asked, So, yes?

grounding: A young Indian abroad notices that head-wobbling, a salary question and a loud call may surprise hosts, and explains kindly and adapts.

subtopic: Global cultures: eye contact, personal space, directness and time
passage: I'm Madhuri, and I work two desks from Gurpreet at a software firm in Toronto. In Gurpreet's first week I watched a small scene. Gurpreet asked a new teammate, cheerfully, "So how much do you earn, and are you married?" The teammate blinked, laughed politely and changed the subject. Later, in the lounge, Gurpreet took a call from home and spoke loudly; two people looked up. I can't know how Gurpreet felt about those glances. That afternoon I told Gurpreet quietly that back home those questions show interest, but here many people save them for close friends. Gurpreet nodded slowly and said, "Oh, I see." The next day Gurpreet asked the teammate about the weekend instead, and calls moved to the corridor.

qa.q: Where does Madhuri work?
qa.a: Madhuri works at a software firm in Toronto.

qa.q: Why did Madhuri speak to Gurpreet quietly that afternoon?
qa.a: To explain kindly without embarrassing Gurpreet, since the questions came from interest, not rudeness.

qa.q: What did Gurpreet change afterwards?
qa.a: Gurpreet asked the teammate about the weekend instead, and moved calls to the corridor.

qa.q: How might Gurpreet have felt about the glances in the lounge?
qa.a: Possibly puzzled or a little self-conscious, though Madhuri cannot know for sure.

grounding: A young Indian abroad sees a colleague's personal questions and loud call surprise hosts and explains kindly, and the colleague adapts.

subtopic: Stereotypes and how to challenge them
passage:
Hansa: Papa, the kids from the next lane are lazy and they never share.
Jeevan: Hmm. Who told you that?
Hansa: Dadaji said it at dinner.
Jeevan: Okay. How do you know it's true?
Hansa: ... I don't know.
Jeevan: Have you played with any of them?
Hansa: No. I only saw them once.
Jeevan: Shall we ask the girl with the red bicycle to play tomorrow?
Hansa: Okay. But what if she doesn't share?
Jeevan: Then we'll see what she does, not what people say.

qa.q: Who said it at dinner?
qa.a: Dadaji said it at dinner.

qa.q: Why did Hansa say the kids from the next lane are lazy?
qa.a: Hansa was repeating Dadaji's words with no evidence of Hansa's own; the answer I don't know shows the words were borrowed.

qa.q: What did Jeevan suggest to test the idea?
qa.a: Asking the girl with the red bicycle to play, then seeing what she actually does.

qa.q: How might the girl with the red bicycle feel if she were called lazy?
qa.a: Hurt or confused, since nobody had even played with her yet.

grounding: A young child repeats that a group is lazy, echoing what was heard at home, and a calm question asks how Hansa knows.

subtopic: Stereotypes and how to challenge them
passage: Note from Manjula, class teacher, about Yusuf, age five. At snack time today Yusuf said the children from the other class are greedy and always take the biggest pieces. I asked, "How do you know?" Yusuf thought for a long while and then said, "My uncle says." Yusuf had not sat with any of them. I invited two children from the other class to share a fruit plate at Yusuf's table. Yusuf cut the pieces evenly and giggled. I will speak gently with Yusuf's family at pickup, share what happened, and not blame anyone.

qa.q: What did Yusuf say when asked how Yusuf knew?
qa.a: Yusuf said, My uncle says.

qa.q: What does Yusuf's long thinking suggest?
qa.a: That Yusuf realised there was no evidence of Yusuf's own, so the idea was borrowed.

qa.q: What did Manjula do next?
qa.a: Manjula invited two children from the other class to share fruit and planned to speak gently with the family without blame.

qa.q: How might the children from the other class feel about being called greedy?
qa.a: Confused or hurt, since they were labelled without being known.

grounding: A child repeats that a group is greedy, echoing words heard at home, and a calm question invites evidence.

subtopic: Stereotypes and how to challenge them
passage: At lunch break under the banyan tree, Ojas's friends began mimicking the way Pema spoke, stretching the words in a sing-song voice. Pema was new, from a far-off hill town. "Say something, Pema, say it!" they laughed. Ojas laughed too, loudly, because everyone did and it felt warm. Then Ojas saw Pema stare at the rice and go quiet. The laugh stuck in Ojas's throat. Anirban had not laughed at all. Anirban simply moved along the bench, sat beside Pema and said, "Tell me about the hill town? I've never seen one." Ojas watched and felt small. The next day Ojas sat there too.

qa.q: Where did the friends have lunch?
qa.a: The friends had lunch under the banyan tree.

qa.q: How did Ojas feel on seeing Pema go quiet?
qa.a: Guilty and uneasy; the laugh stuck in the throat and Ojas felt small.

qa.q: What could Ojas do next time a joke like this starts?
qa.a: Not laugh, and sit beside the person it hurts or change the subject, as Anirban did.

qa.q: What was it like for Pema when friends copied the way Pema spoke?
qa.a: Hurtful and lonely; staring at the rice and going quiet show it.

grounding: A child laughs at mimicry of a classmate's accent because friends do, while another child who does not laugh shows a different way.

subtopic: Stereotypes and how to challenge them
passage: In the Leeds school corridor, Kyle told a joke about people from the countryside who can't work a phone. His friends howled. Jana laughed loudly too, mostly to keep up. Mila, who had moved from a farming village that term, was standing at the locker right beside them, and her smile went stiff. Gabriel did not laugh. "That one's not funny to me," Gabriel said quietly. "Mila is right here." Kyle shrugged and changed the subject. Jana's cheeks burned, then Jana walked over. "Sorry, Mila. I laughed and I shouldn't have." Mila nodded slowly. At lunch, Jana sat with Mila and Gabriel.

qa.q: Where did Kyle tell the joke?
qa.a: Kyle told the joke in the school corridor.

qa.q: Why did Jana laugh at the joke?
qa.a: To keep up with the group, since laughing felt like belonging, though the burning cheeks later showed regret.

qa.q: What could Jana do differently next time?
qa.a: Not laugh, or say quietly that it isn't funny like Gabriel, and check on Mila.

qa.q: How did Mila feel when the joke was told?
qa.a: Hurt and awkward; her smile went stiff.

grounding: A child laughs at a joke about a region because friends do, though someone hurt is present, and a friend who does not laugh shows another way.

subtopic: Stereotypes and how to challenge them
passage: Sonali was showing photos from the Class 10 trip when she pointed at Jahnavi. "You people from your state are all loud and never on time, aren't you?" A few classmates laughed. Jahnavi felt like a photo cropped down to one corner. Jahnavi had been on time every day that week and was quiet in most classes. "That isn't me," Jahnavi said, "and it isn't everyone from home either. My cousin is the quietest person I know." Sonali blinked. "Oh. I just heard it somewhere." At lunch Riya sat beside Jahnavi and said, "Glad you spoke up." For the first time that week Jahnavi's shoulders dropped.

qa.q: How did Jahnavi answer when the label was made?
qa.a: Jahnavi said, That isn't me, and it isn't everyone from home either.

qa.q: How did Jahnavi feel when Sonali pointed, and what does the photo image show?
qa.a: Unseen and reduced; feeling like a photo cropped to one corner shows being seen as one label instead of a whole person.

qa.q: What helped Jahnavi afterwards?
qa.a: Correcting the label calmly with a personal example, and Riya sitting beside Jahnavi at lunch.

qa.q: Why might Sonali have made the remark?
qa.a: Sonali had heard it somewhere and repeated it without thinking; the surprised blink suggests it was borrowed, not personal.

grounding: A teenager is told all people from their state are a certain way, feels unseen, and gently corrects it with supportive peers.

subtopic: Stereotypes and how to challenge them
passage:
At the hockey club after practice, in the changing area:
Swati: You're from that community, right? Everyone from there is stingy.
Rashmi: Sorry? Say that again?
Swati: I mean, that's just what people say.
Rashmi: I bought the whole team samosas last week. And my grandfather runs a free water stall every summer.
Swati: Okay, but that's you.
Rashmi: Exactly. It's me. Do you want to know me, or the label?
Swati: ...Fair. I'm sorry.
Neha, who had been lacing shoes on the bench, looked up. "Rashmi, sit with me at lunch tomorrow?"
Rashmi: Thanks, Neha. I'd like that.

qa.q: What did Rashmi buy for the whole team last week?
qa.a: Rashmi bought samosas for the whole team.

qa.q: How did Rashmi feel on hearing that everyone from there is stingy?
qa.a: Hurt and unseen, and a little angry; Rashmi asked Swati to say it again and answered with facts about Rashmi's own life.

qa.q: What worked in how Rashmi answered?
qa.a: Personal examples and the question of whether Swati wanted to know Rashmi or the label, without attacking.

qa.q: What might Neha's invitation to lunch mean to Rashmi?
qa.a: That Rashmi is not alone, which helps a person feel seen.

grounding: A teenager is told everyone from their community is stingy, feels unseen, and answers with personal examples and finds support.

subtopic: Stereotypes and how to challenge them
passage: Looking back, it started at the cinema with my friend Rehana. Halfway through the film I whispered, "Did you notice the maid is always the one who trips and gets laughed at?" Rehana grinned. "And the villain always has the same beard." We began counting on the walk home. In the next three films: a cook who was a joke, a driver who was a joke, a bad guy in a cap. The hero was nearly always from one kind of family. We started asking, "Who's missing? Who gets to be the main person?" I felt relieved to have words for something I'd felt but couldn't say. It didn't ruin films; it just made me watch with both eyes. Minakshi

qa.q: What did Minakshi and Rehana start doing on the walk home?
qa.a: They began counting the maids, cooks, drivers and villains from the films.

qa.q: How did Minakshi feel once there were words for the pattern?
qa.a: Relieved, because the words named something felt but never said.

qa.q: What question could a viewer ask next?
qa.a: Who is missing, and who gets to be the main person?

qa.q: How did Rehana take Minakshi's first whisper?
qa.a: Rehana grinned and added a point about the villain, showing the pattern had been noticed too.

grounding: A teenager notices films showing some groups as servants, villains or jokes and asks who is missing from the story.

subtopic: Stereotypes and how to challenge them
passage: Film club note, Aditi (teacher). During Friday's screening Charu, 15, pointed out that the shopkeeper, the servant and the villain in three different films all spoke with the same accent and never had a family or a full name. Charu asked the group, "Who is missing from this story? Who never gets to be the hero?" Several students went quiet, then began listing other examples. I did not give an answer. I asked them to watch the next film for who speaks first and who is only in the background. Charu seemed relieved to have the room take it seriously. Next week I will ask them to find one film that does it differently.

qa.q: How old is Charu?
qa.a: Charu is 15.

qa.q: How did Charu seem to feel when the room took the question seriously?
qa.a: Relieved, having noticed a pattern and been heard.

qa.q: What did Aditi ask the students to do next?
qa.a: Watch the next film for who speaks first and who is only in the background.

qa.q: How might the other students in the club have reacted to Charu's question?
qa.a: They went quiet, then began listing other examples, which suggests the question made them think.

grounding: A teenager notices groups shown as villains, servants or comic relief and asks who is missing; a teacher supports critical viewing.

subtopic: Stereotypes and how to challenge them
passage: At the bus stand, a young man in a torn black hoodie with tattoos on his arm and earphones sat beside Joseph. Joseph gripped his bag and shifted along the bench. His hand checked the wallet in his pocket twice. Then the wallet slipped onto the ground without Joseph noticing. The young man tapped his shoulder. "Bhai, your wallet." Joseph took it, face hot, and mumbled thanks. "Karthik," the stranger said, and went back to his tune. Joseph thought: why did I decide all that from a hoodie? It was a cold, honest thought, not a whipping. On the bus Joseph promised to catch the next assumption sooner, and asked Karthik which stop was his.

qa.q: What did the young man say when he tapped Joseph's shoulder?
qa.a: The young man said, Bhai, your wallet.

qa.q: How did Joseph feel gripping the bag, and later?
qa.a: Uneasy and suspicious at first, then embarrassed; the face went hot after the wallet was returned.

qa.q: What was healthy about how Joseph dealt with the bias?
qa.a: Joseph noticed the assumption honestly, without harsh self-punishment, and decided to catch it sooner.

qa.q: How might Karthik have seen Joseph's gripped bag?
qa.a: As unfair suspicion, possibly hurtful, though Karthik still returned the wallet.

grounding: A young adult realises he assumed a stranger would behave a certain way from dress, and notices the bias honestly.

subtopic: Stereotypes and how to challenge them
passage: On a tram in Lisbon, Rosa moved her bag to the far side when a man in a long coat and scarf sat beside her, speaking low on the phone in a language she couldn't place. Her stomach tightened. Each stop felt long. Then a small boy across the aisle dropped a mitten. The man picked it up, smiled and handed it back. Then he turned to Rosa. "You dropped your ticket," he said, holding it out. "I'm Tuan, by the way." Rosa thanked him and felt her cheeks warm. What did I actually see? A coat and a language. She moved the bag back onto her lap, said, "Nice to meet you," and made a note to notice sooner next time.

qa.q: What did Rosa move to the far side?
qa.a: Rosa moved her bag to the far side.

qa.q: What was Rosa feeling when her stomach tightened, and what did she later notice?
qa.a: Anxious and wary; later she noticed she had judged from a coat and a language.

qa.q: How could Rosa treat this without self-punishment?
qa.a: Name the assumption honestly, move the bag back, be friendly, and try to notice sooner next time.

qa.q: How might Tuan have felt seeing the bag moved away?
qa.a: Possibly hurt or uncomfortable, though Tuan still helped by returning the ticket.

grounding: A young adult realises she assumed a stranger would behave a certain way from clothing and language, and notices it honestly.

subtopic: Stereotypes and how to challenge them
passage: In the coaching centre canteen in Delhi, Harish clapped Parul on the back. "You'll top the maths test, obviously. People from your community are naturally good at maths." Parul smiled tightly. The paper in Parul's bag had a red 42 on it from that morning, and nobody knew. Every praise like that was another stone in the bag: if Parul failed, it would look like proof of something. "Thank you, Harish, but I do have to work at it. I got 42 today." Harish paused. "Oh. I didn't know. Sorry. Want to go through it together?" Parul felt the shoulders loosen. "Yes, please."

qa.q: What mark did Parul get that morning?
qa.a: Parul got a red 42.

qa.q: How did Parul feel about the praise?
qa.a: Pressured and trapped; each praise felt like another stone in the bag, since failing would look like proof of something.

qa.q: How did Parul handle the praise wisely?
qa.a: Parul thanked Harish, kindly corrected the assumption and shared the real mark, which led to an offer of help.

qa.q: How might Harish have felt on hearing the mark?
qa.a: Surprised and a little embarrassed, then willing to help.

grounding: A young adult praised as naturally good at maths because of community feels pressure and kindly corrects the assumption.

subtopic: Stereotypes and how to challenge them
passage:
In the office pantry, Jatin leaned on the counter.
Jatin: Manoj, you'll handle the accounts audit, right? Your community's always been hardworking. You people never quit.
Manoj: Thanks, I think. But I'm not sure I'm the right person.
Jatin: Come on, it's in you.
Manoj: It really isn't a gene. I'm tired, and I'm behind on my own work.
Jatin: I didn't think about that. I was trying to be nice.
Manoj: I know. It's just that when everyone expects me to be perfect, I can't say I'm struggling.
Jatin: Okay. Let's split it. You do the first half, I'll do the rest.
Manoj: That would be a relief. Thanks.

qa.q: How does Jatin propose to split the audit?
qa.a: Manoj does the first half and Jatin does the rest.

qa.q: What was Manoj feeling about the expectation, and why?
qa.a: Weighed down and afraid to admit struggling, because everyone expects perfection.

qa.q: What did Manoj do well when replying to the compliment?
qa.a: Manoj stayed kind, said hard work is not a gene, and was honest about being tired.

qa.q: How might Jatin have meant the remark?
qa.a: As a kind compliment, not to pressure Manoj, though it landed heavily.

grounding: A young adult praised as hardworking because of community feels unable to fail and kindly corrects it.
